Learning Objectives

Apply resampling and alignment methodically and correctly

title: 1  1 Classification: Time Series as a Measurement Process
text:
2.1 1.1 Creating a Working Dataset
We create a synthetic time series with:

Trend

Daily periodicity

Noise

Outliers

This structure is typical for real-world technical measurement data.

Pandas (recommended)NumPy (Principle)



import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

# Time index: 14 days, hourly measurements
t = pd.date_range("2025-01-01", periods=24*14, freq="h")

trend = np.linspace(0, 3, len(t))
season = 0.8 * np.sin(2*np.pi*(t.hour)/24)
noise = 0.25 * rng.normal(size=len(t))

y = 10 + trend + season + noise
y = pd.Series(y, index=t, name="signal")

# artificial outliers
y.iloc[50] += 3.5
y.iloc[120] -= 2.8

y.plot()
plt.title("Time Series (Trend + Seasonality + Noise)")
plt.xlabel("Time")
plt.ylabel("Value")
plt.show()










Here we model time as a simple sample index.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

n = 24*14
x = np.arange(n)

trend = np.linspace(0, 3, n)
season = 0.8 * np.sin(2*np.pi*(x % 24)/24)
noise = 0.25 * rng.normal(size=n)

y = 10 + trend + season + noise

# Outliers
y[50] += 3.5
y[120] -= 2.8

plt.plot(y)
plt.title("Time series (NumPy, without time index)")
plt.xlabel("Sample")
plt.ylabel("Value")
plt.show()

2.2 1.2 Typical Analysis Questions
In time series analysis, similar questions arise repeatedly:

Is there a trend?
Does a periodicity exist (e.g., daily or weekly patterns)?
How strong is the noise?
Are there anomalies?
How can future values be roughly estimated?







TipMethodological Perspective



Before smoothing or modeling:

Visualize

Check the time scale

Identify the structure

Only then continue with further analysis

text:
2.3 1.3 Structural Model of a Time Series
A time series can often be conceptually represented as:
Signal = Trend + Seasonality + Noise + Outliers
This decomposition is not a physical law, but rather a conceptual model that helps analyze patterns systematically.






WarningAttention



Not every recurring pattern is automatically “seasonality”.
Regularity must plausibly match the sampling rate and the underlying process.

Before a time series is analyzed, it must be formally correct and consistent.
Many errors in later analyses arise from:

title: 2  2 Preprocessing & Validation of a Time Series

3.1 2.1 Example Time Series with Problems
We intentionally create a faulty time series (unsorted, duplicates, missing values).

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)

t = pd.date_range("2025-01-01", periods=24*3, freq="h")
y = pd.Series(10 + rng.normal(size=len(t)), index=t, name="signal")

# create problems
y = y.sample(frac=1)                      # unsorted
y = pd.concat([y, y.iloc[5:8]])           # duplicates (append is deprecated/removed)
y.iloc[10:15] = np.nan                    # missing values

title: 3  3 Resampling & Alignment
text:
4 3 Resampling & Alignment
Time series often come at different sampling rates or need to be transformed to a different time scale.
Common reasons:

title: 3  3 Resampling & Alignment
text:
4.1 3.1 Original Time Series (Hourly)

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(2)

t = pd.date_range("2025-01-01", periods=24*5, freq="h")
y = pd.Series(10 + rng.normal(size=len(t)), index=t, name="signal")

y.plot(title="Hourly Time Series")
plt.show()

title: 3  3 Resampling & Alignment
text:
4.2 3.2 Downsampling (Aggregation)
We aggregate from hours to days.

daily_mean = y.resample("D").mean()
daily_max = y.resample("D").max()

ax = daily_mean.plot(marker="o", label="Daily Mean")
daily_max.plot(ax=ax, marker="o", label="Daily Maximum")
plt.legend()
plt.title("Downsampling: Hours → Days")
plt.show()















TipDecision Guide




Mean → smooths out fluctuations

Maximum → highlights extreme values

Sum → useful for quantities (e.g., energy consumption)

title: 3  3 Resampling & Alignment
text:
4.3 3.3 Upsampling (Interpolation)
We increase the temporal resolution.

y_2h = y.resample("2h").mean()
y_up = y_2h.resample("h").interpolate("time")

ax = y_2h.plot(marker="o", label="2H (aggregated)")
y_up.plot(ax=ax, alpha=0.7, label="Interpolated to 1H")
plt.legend()
plt.title("Upsampling with Interpolation")
plt.show()















WarningWarning



Interpolation does not generate new measurement data; it only models a plausible progression.

title: 3  3 Resampling & Alignment
text:
4.4 3.4 Alignment of Two Time Series
Two time series with different sampling rates:

t2 = pd.date_range("2025-01-01", periods=24*5, freq="2h")
y2 = pd.Series(5 + rng.normal(size=len(t2)), index=t2, name="signal2")

For joint analysis, both series must have the same frequency.

y2_aligned = y2.resample("h").interpolate("time")

df = pd.concat([y, y2_aligned], axis=1)

df.plot(title="Aligned Time Series")
plt.show()















NoteNote



Alignment means: - same frequency - same time span - same time zone

title: 3  3 Resampling & Alignment
text:
4.5 3.5 Common Sources of Error

Comparisons without prior resampling
Mixing local time and UTC
Aggregation without considering data types (e.g., sum vs mean)

title: 4  4 Smoothing & Noise Reduction
text:
5 4 Smoothing & Noise Reduction
Smoothing is one of the most important standard techniques in time series analysis.
It helps to:

title: 4  4 Smoothing & Noise Reduction
text:
5.1 4.1 Example Signal
We use a time series with a daily pattern, noise, and individual outliers.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

t = pd.date_range("2025-01-01", periods=24*10, freq="h")  # 10 days hourly
trend = np.linspace(0, 2, len(t))
season = 0.9 * np.sin(2*np.pi*(t.hour)/24)
noise = 0.35 * rng.normal(size=len(t))

s = pd.Series(10 + trend + season + noise, index=t, name="signal")

# Outliers
s.iloc[30] += 3.0
s.iloc[120] -= 2.5

s.plot(title="Example Signal (raw)")
plt.show()

title: 4  4 Smoothing & Noise Reduction
text:
5.2 4.2 Rolling Mean
The rolling mean is the classic smoothing method: the average over a window.

Pandas (recommended)NumPy (principle)



roll_6h = s.rolling("6h").mean()
roll_24h = s.rolling("24h").mean()

ax = s.plot(alpha=0.45, label="Signal")
roll_6h.plot(ax=ax, label="Rolling 6H")
roll_24h.plot(ax=ax, label="Rolling 24H")
plt.legend()
plt.title("Rolling Mean (Pandas)")
plt.show()














TipDecision aid




6H: reduces short-term noise, events remain visible
24H: shows basic level/trend, strongly dampens daily patterns





NumPy variant: moving average as convolution (convolve).

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

y = s.to_numpy()

def moving_average(y, window):
    kernel = np.ones(window) / window
    return np.convolve(y, kernel, mode="same")

ma_6 = moving_average(y, 6)
ma_24 = moving_average(y, 24)

plt.plot(y, alpha=0.45, label="Signal")
plt.plot(ma_6, label="MA 6 Samples")
plt.plot(ma_24, label="MA 24 Samples")
plt.legend()
plt.title("Moving Average (NumPy)")
plt.xlabel("Sample")
plt.ylabel("Value")
plt.show()














WarningAttention



When convolving, you must consciously accept edge handling (here: mode=“same”). Pandas handles edge areas consistently with min_periods and NaNs.

title: 4  4 Smoothing & Noise Reduction
text:
5.3 4.3 EWMA (Exponentially Weighted Moving Average)
EWMA smooths, but weights newer values more heavily.

Pandas (recommended)NumPy (Concept)



ewm_fast = s.ewm(span=6, adjust=False).mean()
ewm_slow = s.ewm(span=24, adjust=False).mean()

ax = s.plot(alpha=0.45, label="Signal")
ewm_fast.plot(ax=ax, label="EWMA span=6")
ewm_slow.plot(ax=ax, label="EWMA span=24")
plt.legend()
plt.title("EWMA (Pandas)")
plt.show()














NoteNote



EWMA reacts faster to changes than a rolling mean, because older values have exponentially less influence.




EWMA can be calculated recursively:
[ m_t = y_t + (1-)m_{t-1} ]

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

y = s.to_numpy()

def ewma(y, alpha):
    m = np.empty_like(y, dtype=float)
    m[0] = y[0]
    for i in range(1, len(y)):
        m[i] = alpha * y[i] + (1 - alpha) * m[i-1]
    return m

m_fast = ewma(y, alpha=0.30)
m_slow = ewma(y, alpha=0.08)

plt.plot(y, alpha=0.45, label="Signal")
plt.plot(m_fast, label="EWMA alpha=0.30")
plt.plot(m_slow, label="EWMA alpha=0.08")
plt.legend()
plt.title("EWMA (NumPy)")
plt.xlabel("Sample")
plt.ylabel("Value")
plt.show()

title: 4  4 Smoothing & Noise Reduction
text:
5.4 4.4 Method Choice: Which Approach When?






TipDecision Aid



Rolling Mean is suitable when…
- You want to average over a clearly defined time window (e.g., “last 24 hours”).
EWMA is suitable when…
- You want a smooth baseline that reacts more quickly to changes.
- You want to detect anomalies as deviations from a dynamic baseline.

text:

title: 5  5 Trend & Season
text:
6 5 Trend & Season
Many time series contain systematic structures:
This decomposition is a conceptual model that helps to systematically analyze structure.

title: 5  5 Trend & Season
text:
6.1 5.1 Example Signal

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(10)

t = pd.date_range("2025-01-01", periods=24*14, freq="h")
trend = np.linspace(0, 4, len(t))
season = 1.2 * np.sin(2*np.pi*(t.hour)/24)
noise = 0.4 * rng.normal(size=len(t))

s = pd.Series(20 + trend + season + noise, index=t, name="signal")

s.plot(title="Signal with Trend and Daily Season")
plt.show()

title: 5  5 Trend & Season
text:
6.2 5.2 Visualizing the Season

6.2.1 Hourly Average

season_hour = s.groupby(s.index.hour).mean()

season_hour.plot(marker="o")
plt.title("Average Daily Profile (0–23h)")
plt.xlabel("Hour")
plt.ylabel("Average")
plt.show()














TipInterpretation



A periodic pattern in this visualization suggests a daily seasonality.

title: 5  5 Trend & Season
text:
6.3 5.3 Estimating the Trend (Strong Smoothing)

PandasNumPy (Concept)



trend_est = s.rolling("72h").mean()

ax = s.plot(alpha=0.4, label="Signal")
trend_est.plot(ax=ax, linewidth=2, label="Trend (Rolling 72H)")
plt.legend()
plt.title("Trend Estimation")
plt.show()











import numpy as np

y = s.to_numpy()

def moving_average(y, window):
    kernel = np.ones(window) / window
    return np.convolve(y, kernel, mode="same")

trend_np = moving_average(y, 72)

plt.plot(y, alpha=0.4, label="Signal")
plt.plot(trend_np, linewidth=2, label="Trend (MA 72)")
plt.legend()
plt.title("Trend Estimation (NumPy)")
plt.show()

title: 5  5 Trend & Season
text:
6.4 5.4 Calculating the Residual (Simplified Decomposition)
We roughly remove the trend and seasonality:

season_map = s.index.hour.map(season_hour)
residual = s - trend_est - season_map

residual.plot(title="Residual (Simplified Decomposition)")
plt.show()















WarningWarning



This decomposition is didactically simplified.
In practice, more robust methods exist (e.g., STL).
Here, the focus is on the principle.

title: 5  5 Trend & Season
text:
6.5 5.5 Additive vs Multiplicative Model
Additive model:
Signal = Trend + Season + Noise
Multiplicative model:
Signal = Trend × Season × Noise
Multiplicative models make sense
when the amplitude of the season grows with the level.

text:

title: 6  6 Lags & Autocorrelation
text:
7 6 Lags & Autocorrelation
Time series differ from classical datasets because observations are not independent.
The value at time t often depends on previous values.
We examine this temporal dependence using:

title: 6  6 Lags & Autocorrelation
text:
7.1 6.1 Example Signal

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(21)

t = pd.date_range("2025-01-01", periods=24*14, freq="h")
trend = np.linspace(0, 2, len(t))
season = 0.8 * np.sin(2*np.pi*(t.hour)/24)
noise = 0.4 * rng.normal(size=len(t))

s = pd.Series(15 + trend + season + noise, index=t, name="signal")

s.plot(title="Example Signal")
plt.show()

title: 6  6 Lags & Autocorrelation
text:
7.2 6.2 Lag Features
A lag shifts the time series backward.

PandasNumPy (Concept)



lag_1h = s.shift(1)
lag_24h = s.shift(24)

df_lags = pd.DataFrame({
    "y": s,
    "lag_1h": lag_1h,
    "lag_24h": lag_24h
})

title: 6  6 Lags & Autocorrelation
text:
7.3 6.3 Calculating Autocorrelation
Autocorrelation measures the correlation between y(t) and y(t-k).

PandasNumPy (Principle)



lags = range(1, 49)
ac = [s.corr(s.shift(k)) for k in lags]

plt.stem(list(lags), ac)
plt.title("Autocorrelation (1–48 hours)")
plt.xlabel("Lag (h)")
plt.ylabel("Correlation")
plt.show()











import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

y = s.to_numpy()
y = y - np.nanmean(y)

def autocorr(y, k):
    return np.corrcoef(y[:-k], y[k:])[0,1]

lags = range(1, 49)
ac_np = [autocorr(y, k) for k in lags]

plt.stem(list(lags), ac_np)
plt.title("Autocorrelation (NumPy)")
plt.xlabel("Lag")
plt.ylabel("Correlation")
plt.show()

title: 6  6 Lags & Autocorrelation
text:
7.4 6.4 Interpretation of Autocorrelation
Typical patterns:

Slowly decreasing curve → strong trend
Periodic peaks (e.g., at 24, 48, 72) → seasonality
Rapid drop toward 0 → weak dependence








WarningWarning



A trend can artificially increase autocorrelation.
If necessary, first detrend or difference the series.

text:

title: 7  7 Anomalies
text:
8 7 Anomalies
Anomalies are observations that deviate significantly from expected behavior.
In time series this means:
Important: anomalies are context-dependent.

title: 7  7 Anomalies
text:
8.1 7.1 Example Signal with Outliers

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(99)

t = pd.date_range("2025-01-01", periods=24*10, freq="h")
trend = np.linspace(0, 2, len(t))
season = 0.8 * np.sin(2*np.pi*(t.hour)/24)
noise = 0.3 * rng.normal(size=len(t))

s = pd.Series(10 + trend + season + noise, index=t, name="signal")

# artificial anomalies
s.iloc[40] += 4
s.iloc[120] -= 3

s.plot(title="Signal with Anomalies")
plt.show()

title: 7  7 Anomalies
text:
8.2 7.2 Global Z-Score Method
We standardize the entire time series.

PandasNumPy



z = (s - s.mean()) / s.std()
anomalies = s[abs(z) > 3]

ax = s.plot(label="Signal")
anomalies.plot(ax=ax, linestyle="None", marker="o", label="Anomaly")
plt.legend()
plt.title("Anomalies (Z-Score)")
plt.show()











y = s.to_numpy()

z_np = (y - np.mean(y)) / np.std(y)
anomalies_idx = np.where(np.abs(z_np) > 3)[0]

plt.plot(y, label="Signal")
plt.scatter(anomalies_idx, y[anomalies_idx], label="Anomaly")
plt.legend()
plt.title("Anomalies (NumPy Z-Score)")
plt.show()


















WarningWarning



Z-score performs poorly when there is a strong trend or seasonality, because global means can become distorted.

title: 7  7 Anomalies
text:
8.3 7.3 Local Anomaly (Baseline + Residual)
Instead of global standardization, we define a local baseline.

baseline = s.ewm(span=24, adjust=False).mean()
residual = s - baseline

score = (residual - residual.mean()) / residual.std()
anomalies_local = s[abs(score) > 3]

ax = s.plot(alpha=0.6, label="Signal")
baseline.plot(ax=ax, label="Baseline")
anomalies_local.plot(ax=ax, linestyle="None", marker="o", label="Anomaly")
plt.legend()
plt.title("Local Anomalies (EWMA Baseline)")
plt.show()















TipInterpretation



Local methods are more robust when a trend or seasonality is present.

title: 7  7 Anomalies
text:
8.4 7.4 Rolling Standard Deviation
Anomalies can also be defined as strong deviations relative to the local variance.

rolling_std = s.rolling("24h").std()
rolling_mean = s.rolling("24h").mean()

upper = rolling_mean + 3 * rolling_std
lower = rolling_mean - 3 * rolling_std

ax = s.plot(label="Signal")
upper.plot(ax=ax, linestyle="--", label="Upper Bound")
lower.plot(ax=ax, linestyle="--", label="Lower Bound")
plt.legend()
plt.title("Anomalies via Rolling Bounds")
plt.show()

title: 7  7 Anomalies
text:

A single peak → Outlier
A permanent level shift → Structural Break
Both require different interpretation.

title: 8  8 Forecasting Baselines & Evaluation
text:
9 8 Forecasting Baselines & Evaluation
Before applying complex models, simple baseline models should always be defined.
Baselines answer the question:

title: 8  8 Forecasting Baselines & Evaluation
text:
9.1 8.1 Example Time Series

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(123)

t = pd.date_range("2025-01-01", periods=24*14, freq="h")
trend = np.linspace(0, 2, len(t))
season = 0.9 * np.sin(2*np.pi*(t.hour)/24)
noise = 0.3 * rng.normal(size=len(t))

s = pd.Series(20 + trend + season + noise, index=t, name="signal")

s.plot(title="Time Series for Forecasting")
plt.show()

title: 8  8 Forecasting Baselines & Evaluation
text:
9.2 8.2 Train-Test Split
We use 80% of the data for training and 20% for testing.

split = int(len(s) * 0.8)

train = s.iloc[:split]
test = s.iloc[split:]

train.index.min(), train.index.max(), test.index.min(), test.index.max()

(Timestamp('2025-01-01 00:00:00'),
 Timestamp('2025-01-12 03:00:00'),
 Timestamp('2025-01-12 04:00:00'),
 Timestamp('2025-01-14 23:00:00'))

title: 8  8 Forecasting Baselines & Evaluation
text:
9.3 8.3 Naive Forecast
Next value = last observed value.

PandasNumPy



naive = test.copy()
naive[:] = train.iloc[-1]




y = s.to_numpy()
train_np = y[:split]
test_np = y[split:]

naive_np = np.full_like(test_np, train_np[-1])

title: 8  8 Forecasting Baselines & Evaluation
text:
9.4 8.4 Seasonal Naive (24 Hours)
Next value = value from 24 hours ago.

PandasNumPy



seasonal_naive = s.shift(24).iloc[split:]




seasonal_naive_np = y[split-24:-24]

title: 8  8 Forecasting Baselines & Evaluation
text:
9.5 8.5 Moving Average Baseline
Forecast = mean of the last 24 hours.

PandasNumPy



ma_value = train.iloc[-24:].mean()
ma_forecast = test.copy()
ma_forecast[:] = ma_value




ma_value_np = np.mean(train_np[-24:])
ma_forecast_np = np.full_like(test_np, ma_value_np)

title: 8  8 Forecasting Baselines & Evaluation
text:
9.6 8.6 Visualizing Comparison

plt.figure()
train.plot(label="Train")
test.plot(label="Test")
naive.plot(label="Naive")
seasonal_naive.plot(label="Seasonal Naive")
ma_forecast.plot(label="MA(24)")
plt.legend()
plt.title("Forecast Baselines")
plt.show()

title: 8  8 Forecasting Baselines & Evaluation
text:
9.7 8.7 Error Metrics
We use the Mean Absolute Error (MAE):
\[
MAE = \frac{1}{n} \sum |y_{true} - y_{pred}|
\]

PandasNumPy



def mae(y_true, y_pred):
    return np.mean(np.abs(y_true - y_pred))

print("MAE Naive:", mae(test, naive))
print("MAE Seasonal Naive:", mae(test, seasonal_naive))
print("MAE MA(24):", mae(test, ma_forecast))

MAE Naive: 0.6298837368696829
MAE Seasonal Naive: 0.3320412574311427
MAE MA(24): 0.6228787570177815





def mae_np(y_true, y_pred):
    return np.mean(np.abs(y_true - y_pred))

print("MAE Naive:", mae_np(test_np, naive_np))
print("MAE Seasonal:", mae_np(test_np, seasonal_naive_np))
print("MAE MA(24):", mae_np(test_np, ma_forecast_np))

MAE Naive: 0.6298837368696829
MAE Seasonal: 0.3320412574311427
MAE MA(24): 0.6228787570177815

title: 8  8 Forecasting Baselines & Evaluation
text:
9.8 8.8 Interpretation
Typical observations:

With a strong seasonal pattern, Seasonal Naive often performs best.
With a weak pattern, Naive can be surprisingly strong.
Moving Average smooths the data but reacts slowly to trend changes.








TipMethodological Note



Comparing to a baseline is not a formality, but a quality check.
